q: What is health insurance?
r: Coverage that pays part of the cost of medical care
Members pay premiums and cost sharing.
w: A loan to pay hospital bills

q: What is a premium?
r: The amount paid regularly to keep an insurance policy active
It is paid whether or not care is used.
w: The amount paid before coverage begins each year
The fee paid at each visit
The limit an insurer will pay

q: What is an out-of-pocket maximum?
r: The most a member pays in a year for covered care
After that the plan pays covered costs in full.
w: The least a member pays for insurance
The most an insurer pays for a lifetime

q: What is a claim?
r: A request sent to an insurer for payment of services
Providers submit claims after care.
w: A patient's complaint about a doctor

q: What is a CMS-1500 form used for?
r: Billing insurers for services provided by physicians and suppliers
It is a standard claim form.

q: What is medical coding?
r: Converting diagnoses and procedures into standard codes for billing and records
Codes allow consistent reporting.

q: What do ICD-10 codes represent?
r: Diagnoses and conditions
They describe the reason for care.

q: What do CPT codes represent?
r: Procedures and services provided to patients
They describe what was done.

q: A claim lists a diagnosis code and a procedure code. What does the diagnosis code show?
r: Why the service was needed
It supports medical necessity.

q: What is medical necessity?
r: Services that are reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition
Insurers pay for necessary care.
w: Services that are the most expensive

q: What is prior authorization?
r: Insurer approval required before certain services or drugs are provided
Without it, a claim may be denied.

q: A procedure needs prior authorization but the office did not get it. What is the likely result?
r: The insurer may deny the claim
The provider or patient may owe the cost.
w: The claim is paid with no review

q: What is a referral?
r: A recommendation from a primary provider to see a specialist
Some plans require it.
w: A bill sent to a patient
A medicine prescribed to a patient

q: What is an explanation of benefits (EOB)?
r: A statement from an insurer showing how a claim was processed
It is not a bill.
w: An EOB is not a bill.

q: An EOB shows billed $500, allowed $320 and plan paid $256. What does the patient likely owe?
r: $320 allowed minus $256 paid equals $64.
w: That is the full billed amount.

q: What is the allowed amount?
r: The maximum an insurer will recognize for a covered service
In-network providers accept it as payment.
w: The total a provider chooses to bill

q: What is balance billing?
r: Billing a patient for the difference between the provider's charge and the insurer's payment
Rules limit it in many cases.

q: What is a denied claim?
r: A claim the insurer refuses to pay
Reasons include missing information or no coverage.
w: A claim cancelled by the insurer's office

q: Which is a common reason for claim denial?
r: Missing or incorrect patient information
Clean claims reduce denials.
w: A fully complete and accurate claim
That is more likely to be paid.

q: What is an appeal in billing?
r: A formal request asking an insurer to reconsider a denied claim
Supporting documents are included.
w: A request to cancel a patient's insurance
A request to see a doctor

q: What is a clean claim?
r: A claim with complete and correct information that can be processed without correction
It is paid faster.
w: A claim that has been laundered
A claim printed on white paper
A claim with no patient name

q: What is the typical timeline concept of timely filing?
r: A deadline for submitting a claim to an insurer
Late claims may be denied.
w: A deadline for patients to schedule visits
A deadline for hospitals to pay rent
A deadline for insurance cards to expire

q: What is Medicare?
r: A federal health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older and some with disabilities
It has parts A, B, C and D.
w: A state program for children only
A private plan for employees only

q: What does Medicare Part A mostly cover?
r: Hospital inpatient care and some skilled nursing
It is hospital insurance.

q: What does Medicare Part B mostly cover?
r: Doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive services
It is medical insurance.

q: What is Medicaid?
r: A joint federal and state program that helps cover health costs for people with low income
States run their own programs.
w: A program for hospital employees only

q: What is the main difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
r: Medicare is mostly based on age or disability; Medicaid is based on income
Different groups qualify.
w: Medicare is for children; Medicaid is for adults
Medicare is private; Medicaid is for the military

q: What is TRICARE?
r: A health program for military service members, retirees and their families
The Department of Defense runs it.
w: A program for civil servants only

q: What is coordination of benefits?
r: Determining which insurer pays first when a patient has more than one plan
It prevents overpayment.
w: Sending bills to the government only

q: A child is covered by both parents' plans. Which plan is usually primary?
r: The plan of the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year
This is the birthday rule.
w: The plan of the older parent
The plan of the parent with higher pay
The plan chosen by the child

q: What is a self-pay (cash) patient?
r: A patient who pays for services directly without using insurance
They may receive a discounted rate.

q: What is a flexible spending account (FSA)?
r: An account funded with pre-tax pay to cover eligible health costs
Unused funds may be lost under some rules.

q: What is a health savings account (HSA)?
r: A tax-advantaged account for medical costs used with a high-deductible health plan
Funds roll over each year.

q: Which is a key advantage of an HSA?
r: Contributions, growth and qualified withdrawals can be tax-advantaged
It can also roll over from year to year.
w: It must be spent by the end of every month
It can only be used by employers
It pays for any expense with no rules

q: What does HIPAA stand for?
r: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
It protects health information privacy.
w: Hospital Insurance Payment and Administration Act
Hospital Infection Prevention and Alert Act

q: What is protected health information (PHI)?
r: Individually identifiable health information held by covered entities
Names linked to diagnoses are examples.
w: General health tips on a website

q: Who must follow HIPAA rules?
r: Healthcare providers, health plans and their business associates
They are called covered entities and associates.

q: A nurse looks up a famous patient's record out of curiosity. What is this?
r: A HIPAA violation
Access must be for job-related reasons.

q: What is the HIPAA Privacy Rule mainly about?
r: Who may use and share patients' health information
It protects patient confidentiality.
w: How many beds a hospital has

q: What is the HIPAA Security Rule mainly about?
r: Safeguards for electronic protected health information
It requires administrative, physical and technical protections.

q: Which is a permitted use of PHI without special authorization?
r: Sharing information for treatment, payment and healthcare operations
These purposes are allowed.
w: Posting a patient's diagnosis on social media
Telling a neighbor about a patient's condition

q: What is informed consent?
r: A patient's agreement to treatment after understanding the risks and benefits
The provider must explain clearly.
w: A patient's signature on a blank form
A patient being told after treatment

q: A patient signs a consent form without anyone explaining the procedure. What is the problem?
r: The consent may not be truly informed
Understanding is required.

q: What is an advance directive?
r: A legal document stating a person's wishes for care if they cannot speak for themselves
A living will is one type.

q: What is a Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order?
r: A medical order not to attempt CPR if a patient's heart or breathing stops
It reflects the patient's wishes.
w: An order to try CPR in every case
An order to discharge the patient
An order to refuse all treatment

q: What is the Affordable Care Act (ACA)?
r: A federal law that expanded access to health insurance and set coverage standards
It created marketplaces and protections.
w: A law that bans all private insurance
A law that sets doctor salaries
A law that creates new hospitals

q: Which is a protection under the ACA?
r: Insurers cannot deny coverage because of pre-existing conditions
This protects people with prior illness.
w: Insurers can refuse anyone with a past illness
All care is free for everyone

q: What is the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA)?
r: A law requiring hospitals with emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients regardless of ability to pay
It prevents patient dumping.
w: A law that bans emergency rooms
A law that requires payment before care
A law that limits visitor hours

q: What is the FDA's role in healthcare?
r: Regulating the safety of drugs, medical devices and food
It approves new drugs.

q: What is the role of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)?
r: Administering Medicare and overseeing Medicaid programs
It sets many payment rules.

q: What is the Joint Commission?
r: An independent organization that accredits healthcare organizations on quality and safety
Many hospitals seek its accreditation.
w: A government agency that sets prices
A company that makes medical devices

q: What is a scope of practice?
r: The procedures and actions a licensed professional is legally allowed to perform
States define it.
w: The size of a hospital's campus
The hours a clinic is open

q: A medical assistant begins prescribing drugs. What is the problem?
r: It goes beyond the legal scope of practice
Only authorized prescribers may do this.
w: It is allowed for all staff

q: What is malpractice?
r: Professional negligence that causes harm to a patient
It can lead to a lawsuit.

q: What is the False Claims Act concerned with?
r: Fraudulent billing of government health programs
Submitting false claims can bring penalties.

q: A clinic bills Medicare for services never provided. What is this?
r: Healthcare fraud
Billing for services not rendered is fraud.

q: What is the Stark Law about?
r: Limiting physician referrals to entities they have a financial relationship with
It protects against self-referral abuses.

q: What is the Anti-Kickback Statute about?
r: Banning payments meant to induce referrals for federal healthcare program business
Offering or receiving kickbacks is illegal.

q: What is a mandatory reporter?
r: A person legally required to report suspected abuse or neglect
Many healthcare workers are mandatory reporters.
w: A journalist who writes about hospitals

q: A nurse suspects a child is being abused. What is the nurse's duty?
r: Report the suspicion to the proper authorities as required by law
Failure to report can bring penalties.
w: Ignore it unless the parent confirms
Discuss it with the child's neighbors
